answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the US TIP Report 2023 (covering 2022) shows anti-trafficking units identifying and assisting victims, but labour inspectors lacked training and referred few if any cases. No pattern of employers confiscating documents is documented; enforcement against employer retention comes through trafficking cases. 2026: the starting coder's evidence (migration-police and prosecutor raids in 2024 against employers who held Venezuelan workers' passports; the blanket 'decomiso temporal' of US deportees' passports at CATEM in Feb–Apr 2025, with the passports later returned) shows the same pattern. Retention by private actors is acted on when it surfaces as trafficking; detection outside trafficking is weak; there was one State episode in 2025. The level stays at Usually; no documented shift.

answers.sourcing_note: Every cited provision was read in the current SINALEVI consolidated text, whose per-article amendment notes show no change in force between 1 Jan 2023 and 1 Jan 2026. Labour Code art. 70 was last amended by Ley 10211 of May 2022; Penal Code art. 223 by Ley 6726 of 1982; Ley 9095 art. 6 by Ley 9545 of 2018. The only window amendment, Ley 10493, touches a fee paragraph of art. 33. The 2023 text is therefore the current text minus later notes; no archived version was opened.

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the US Human Rights Report 2022 records statelessness problems for indigenous Ngäbe-Buglé children and children of seasonal workers in the Panama and Nicaragua border areas, arising from difficulties completing birth registration. It also records active TSE–UNHCR mobile registration and late-registration projects. 2026: the US Human Rights Report 2023 repeats the same gaps: migrant children at risk of statelessness when parents do not register them, and border-area seasonal-worker children. It also describes continued joint TSE/UNHCR/IOM registration programmes. The starting coder's TSE procedure sheets show free hospital registration on a foreign passport, with a proof-of-entry requirement for late home-birth registration. Registration is the norm, with known gaps for border and irregular families; no shift between the dates.

events.article: Reglamento de Personas Refugiadas, art. 54 (also art. 14)
events.what_changed: Under the 43810-MGP regime in force on 1 Jan 2023, the asylum seeker's provisional document regularised stay but did not itself authorise work. A separate, employer-tied permit could be sought after 3 months (procedure published Feb 2023). The new art. 54 makes the provisional document valid up to two years and itself grant the right to paid work, employed or self-employed. The document now records work status for asylum seekers.

(Así reformado por el artículo 2° del decreto ejecutivo N° 44501 del 28 de mayo del 2024)

events.what_changed: Changed the paragraph on fee exemptions and reductions; inciso 2 (duty to carry identity and migration documents) untouched. No effect on the indicator.
events.passage: (Así reformado el párrafo anterior por el artículo 1° de la ley N° 10493 del 5 de junio del 2024)

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the US Human Rights Report 2022 says asylum seekers got provisional documents after an interview, with about a two-month wait, and that government authorities generally accepted them while many private actors did not. The 2023 report says that under the 2022 decree new applicants had to wait three months and file extra documentation for work authorisation. 2026: the starting coder's evidence shows the DGME routinely issuing DIMEX and asylum documents but with a backlog of about 20,000 DIMEX cards in late 2025 and early 2026 (Semanario Universidad, Teletica). Since July 2024 the asylum card carries the work permit. Both dates rate Usually (issued as routine, with delays); the legal content changed, not the implementation level.

The difference is that from 14 June 2024 the asylum document itself records work authorisation, which under 43810 was a separate employer-tied permit. Hence 'not the same' rather than 'no change'. answers.implementation_then_now: No report found for either period of officials, employers or others destroying migrants' residence, work or identity documents. The 2023 TIP report (covering 2022) and the starting coder's 2025 TIP report mention no document destruction. In the 2025 CATEM episode (starting coder's evidence, not re-opened here), seized passports were logged, kept in a safe and returned. No prosecution data for arts. 369 or 228 exist for either period, so both ratings rest mainly on the absence of documented breaches; no shift.
